lead: A dynamic gate stores its output on a capacitor instead of holding it with a pull-up network. A clock φ first precharges the dynamic node to V<sub>DD</sub>, then lets an nMOS network discharge it if the inputs say so. An N-input gate needs only N + 2 transistors, and its inputs drive only nMOS, so it is small and fast. The price is a clock on every gate, charge sharing, leakage and the rule that inputs may only rise during evaluation. Domino logic adds an inverter so dynamic gates can be chained, and cascode voltage switch logic (CVSL) gives true and complement outputs from one gate.
prereq: You need: static CMOS and ratioed logic and charge conservation on capacitors.

blocks.text: The dynamic node X connects to V<sub>DD</sub> through a pMOS precharge transistor and to ground through the nMOS pull-down network (PDN) in series with an nMOS evaluate (foot) transistor. Both clock transistors take φ.

items: Precharge (φ = 0): the pMOS is on and the foot is off, so X charges to VDD whatever the inputs.
Evaluate (φ = 1): the pMOS is off and the foot is on. If the PDN conducts, X discharges to 0 V; if not, X stays high, held only by its capacitance CX.

blocks.text: X computes NOT(F) of the PDN function, like a static gate, with full rails and no static current. Once X has fallen it cannot rise again until the next precharge, so an input glitch during evaluation can discharge X wrongly and the error is permanent. Inputs must therefore be stable, or only rise, during evaluation. Because the node floats when the PDN is off, leakage slowly discharges it, which sets a lowest clock frequency.
Some syllabi list clock feedthrough too: the rising clock couples through the gate-drain capacitance of the precharge pMOS and can push X briefly above VDD.

In a stacked PDN, an internal node may be at 0 V from an earlier cycle. If during evaluation the top transistor turns on but the path to ground stays open, X shares its charge with that internal node and drops, even though the output should stay high:
VX = (CXVDD + CintVint)/(CX + Cint) Here cint and Vint are the internal node's capacitance and starting voltage. Total charge is conserved.

If VX falls below the switching threshold of the gate that reads it, the logic fails. Cures: precharge the internal nodes too, keep Cint small, and add a keeper, a weak pMOS from VDD to X whose gate is driven by the output inverter. While X is high the output is low, so the keeper is on and replaces charge lost to leakage and sharing. It must be weak enough that the PDN can still pull X down, which makes the gate slightly ratioed.

A dynamic node is high during precharge. If it drove the nMOS of a second dynamic gate directly, that gate would start evaluating with a false 1 and could discharge wrongly before the first gate settles. Domino logic puts a static inverter after every dynamic node. The domino output is 0 during precharge and can only rise during evaluation, so each stage triggers the next like a row of falling dominoes. A domino gate is non-inverting (AND, OR), so inverting functions need dual-rail signals or are done in static logic at the ends.

np-CMOS (NORA) alternates nMOS-network stages with pMOS-network stages clocked by the inverted clock, so no inverter is needed between them. TSPC (true single-phase clock) logic builds latches and dynamic gates from one clock phase. Only a few syllabi teach these two in detail.

CVSL (also DCVSL) has two nMOS networks, one for F and one for F̄, each pulling down one of two outputs, and two cross-coupled pMOS loads. When one side pulls its output low, it turns on the opposite pMOS, which pulls the other output fully high and turns its own load off. Both outputs swing rail to rail and there is no static current, but during the transition the nMOS must overpower the pMOS, so the sizes are ratioed. CVSL needs complementary inputs and about twice the pull-down transistors; it is used for complex functions such as XOR trees in adders.

examples.question: A domino AND gate has its dynamic node C<sub>X</sub> = 50 fF precharged to 1.8 V. An internal node of 10 fF in the stack is at 0 V. During evaluation the top nMOS turns on but the bottom one stays off. Find V<sub>X</sub>. If the output inverter switches at 1.5 V, what is the largest internal capacitance that is safe?
steps: Charge before: Q = 50 fF × 1.8 V + 10 fF × 0 V = 90 fC.
V<sub>X</sub> = 90 fC / 60 fF = 1.50 V: the drop of 0.30 V brings X right to the inverter's switching point.
Safe limit: V<sub>X</sub> ≥ 1.5 V needs 50 × 1.8/(50 + C<sub>int</sub>) ≥ 1.5, so 50 + C<sub>int</sub> ≤ 60 and C<sub>int</sub> ≤ 10 fF.
So 10 fF is the edge, with no margin; a keeper or precharging the internal node is needed.
examples.answer: V<sub>X</sub> = 1.50 V; any internal capacitance above 10 fF (one fifth of C<sub>X</sub>) makes the gate fail without a keeper.

examples.question: The same dynamic node (50 fF) leaks 10 nA when the PDN is off and there is no keeper. The output stays valid while X loses at most 0.3 V. The node must hold for half a clock period. Find the lowest safe clock frequency.
steps: Hold time = C × ΔV / I = 50 fF × 0.3 V / 10 nA = 15 fC / 10 nA = 1.5 µs.
Half the period must be no longer than 1.5 µs, so T ≤ 3 µs.
examples.answer: The clock must not fall below about 333 kHz; for slower or stopped clocks a keeper is required.

traps: Cascading plain dynamic gates. The precharged high output falsely turns on the next gate; use domino or np-CMOS.
Ignoring charge sharing: X can drop although the pull-down path is open.
Making the keeper strong. It then fights the PDN, slowing or stopping evaluation.
Letting inputs fall during evaluation. A discharged node cannot recover until the next precharge.
Calling CVSL ratioless. The nMOS network must overpower the cross-coupled pMOS while switching.

quiz.q: Name the two phases of a dynamic gate and the state of the clock transistors in each.
quiz.a: Precharge (φ = 0): pMOS on, foot off, X goes to V<sub>DD</sub>. Evaluate (φ = 1): pMOS off, foot on, X discharges if the PDN conducts.

quiz.q: Why does a domino gate need an inverter after its dynamic node?
quiz.a: The inverted output is 0 during precharge and can only rise during evaluation, so it never gives the next stage a false 1; inputs to dynamic gates must not fall during evaluation.

quiz.q: C<sub>X</sub> = 80 fF at 1.8 V shares charge with an internal node of 20 fF at 0 V. Find V<sub>X</sub>.
C<sub>X</sub> = 60 fF at 1.8 V shares with 15 fF at 0.9 V. Find V<sub>X</sub>.
What is the job of the keeper transistor?
quiz.a: A weak pMOS, driven by the output inverter, that holds the dynamic node high against leakage and charge sharing.

quiz.q: How many transistors does a 4-input dynamic NAND need, and a static one?
quiz.a: Dynamic: 4 nMOS + precharge + foot = 6 (8 with a keeper and output inverter). Static CMOS: 8.

quiz.q: Why is CVSL called ratioed during switching, and what does it gain over domino?
quiz.a: While one output is being pulled down, its cross-coupled pMOS is still on, so the nMOS network must be stronger. It gains both F and F̄ with full swing and no clock, so it can implement inverting functions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Domino logic was used in the fastest parts of high-end processors through the 2000s; leakage and variability in nanometre processes have since pushed most designs back to static CMOS. Dynamic circuits survive in register files, SRAM bit lines and sense amplifiers. Search next for clock-delayed domino, footless domino and TSPC flip-flops.

figure.caption: The domino AND gate of the worked examples. When φ is low the precharge pMOS charges X to 1.8 V; when φ is high the foot turns on. If A turns on while B stays off, X shares its charge with the 10 fF internal node and falls to 1.50 V; the weak keeper, driven from the output, tops it back up.

spec.aria: A domino AND gate: a precharge pMOS and a keeper pMOS from VDD to the dynamic node X of 50 femtofarads, an output inverter whose output drives the keeper gate, and below X an nMOS for A, an internal node of 10 femtofarads, an nMOS for B and a clocked foot transistor to ground.
